metaDescription: Five reciprocating saws at or under $150, corded and cordless, compared on stroke length, amps, blade clamp design and platform, from DEWALT to RYOBI.
expertTake: The DEWALT DWE305 is the pick for most demolition work because a 12 amp motor and a 4-position blade clamp keep cutting through nail-embedded studs and pipe all day without a battery fading. The DEWALT DCS387B is the cordless pick for tight spots, since a 14 inch body fits between studs, and the SKIL 9206-02 is the value pick for occasional cuts. Skip this bracket if you cut metal pipe daily, because a corded saw with a larger stroke and a rafter hook will outlast anything here.
introParagraphs: A reciprocating saw pushes and pulls a blade in a straight line, which makes it the tool for demolition, pruning and cutting in places no circular saw can reach. The blade does most of the work, so the saw's job is to hold stroke speed under load and survive the vibration.

This guide explains what a modest budget buys in a reciprocating saw, why stroke length, amps and clamp design matter more than the label, and how corded and cordless models trade endurance for reach. The picks are listed above, with the reviews below. Listing prices move, and the cap reflects prices when this guide was updated.

products.name: DEWALT DWE305 12 Amp Corded Reciprocating Saw, 2,900 SPM
products.description:
A 12 amp motor drives the blade at up to 2,900 strokes per minute, enough to chew through a 2x4 with nails or a 1-1/2 inch pipe without slowing. The keyless lever-action clamp swaps blades in seconds, and four clamp positions let you rotate the blade 90 degrees for flush cuts against a wall or floor. A variable-speed trigger controls the start, which matters because a saw that jumps to full speed can skip off a curved pipe.

The tradeoff is the cord. Compared with the DEWALT DCS380B at 3,000 strokes per minute, the corded saw holds its power without a battery fade, but it needs an outlet and an extension cord. Against the SKIL 9206-02 at 7.5 amps, the DEWALT has nearly 60 percent more motor capacity, which shows in thick or wet lumber. If you do remodeling and tear-out, it is the saw that keeps working.

Ownership: the blade clamp collects dust, so blow it out occasionally. Change blades as soon as the cut slows, because a dull blade heats the motor. Check the brushes after heavy use, and use a blade matched to the job, with fewer teeth for wood and more teeth for metal. A practical tip for any corded saw is to clamp the work or brace it against a stud, because an unsupported board vibrates and chatters the blade in a way that both dulls it and tires your hands.
products.bestFor: Remodelers and demolition users who want sustained corded power at a low relative price.
pros: 12 amp motor holds speed through nails and thick lumber
Four-position clamp allows flush cuts against walls
Keyless lever swaps blades in seconds
No battery to fade during long sessions
cons: Needs an outlet or a heavy extension cord
Heavier than the compact cordless saws
Vibration is higher than orbital-damped saws

products.name: DEWALT DCS387B 20V MAX Compact Reciprocating Saw (Tool Only)
products.description:
A 14 inch overall length lets this saw slip between studs and joists where a full-size saw will not fit. A 1-1/8 inch stroke is long for a compact tool, and it clears chips faster and cuts quicker than a 3/4 inch stroke. The four-position blade clamp allows flush cuts, and an LED lights up the work.

The tradeoff is endurance. A compact cordless saw uses a smaller motor than the DEWALT DWE305, and a long demolition session drains a battery faster than the corded saw would work. Against the DCS380B, the DCS387B is shorter and lighter but has less stroke speed. For plumbing and electrical work in tight spaces, the size outweighs the lower power.

Ownership: this is a bare tool, so you need 20V MAX batteries. A 5.0 Ah pack is a good match for a day of cutting. Keep spare blades in a pouch, since a dull blade drains a battery faster than a fresh one, and store the battery away from heat. For cuts inside a wall cavity, choose a short, thick blade, since a long thin blade whips and snaps when the saw is held at an awkward angle.
products.bestFor: Plumbers and electricians who cut in tight spaces and own 20V MAX batteries.
pros: 14 inch body fits between studs and joists
1-1/8 inch stroke is long for a compact saw
Four-position clamp allows flush cuts
LED lights dark cavities
cons: Tool only, so batteries and a charger cost extra
Less sustained power than a corded saw
Smaller motor drains packs on long demolition jobs

products.name: DEWALT DCS380B 20V MAX Reciprocating Saw, 3,000 SPM (Tool Only)
products.description:
The pivoting adjustable shoe serves two purposes: it extends blade life by letting you use different parts of the blade, and it controls depth of cut. A 1-1/8 inch stroke and 3,000 strokes per minute give fast cutting, and a rubber over-molded grip reduces vibration fatigue. The four-position clamp allows flush cuts like the corded DWE305.

Compared with the DCS387B, this saw is longer and stronger, and it cuts faster, but it does not fit as many tight spaces. The cordless design means you can work on a ladder or roof without an extension cord, and 3,000 SPM matches the corded saw's speed. For tear-out and pruning away from outlets, it is the best cordless option here.

Ownership: another bare tool, so batteries cost extra. Use the shoe to spread wear across the blade, and change blades on schedule. Clean the clamp, and avoid cutting with a nearly empty battery, since voltage sag slows the stroke. Because the pivoting shoe pivots on a hinge, pressing it firmly against the work before squeezing the trigger prevents the saw from jumping, and it lets you roll the blade to use fresh teeth.
products.bestFor: Demolition and pruning users who want cordless speed and already own 20V MAX packs.
pros: 3,000 SPM matches corded speed in a cordless saw
Pivoting shoe extends blade life and controls depth
1-1/8 inch stroke cuts quickly
Rubber grip reduces vibration fatigue
cons: Tool only, so batteries and a charger cost extra
Longer body does not fit as many tight spaces
Large packs add weight on overhead cuts

products.name: RYOBI ONE+ 18V Cordless Reciprocating Saw, 3,400 SPM (Tool Only)
products.description:
A 3,400 strokes per minute top speed is the fastest in this roundup, which helps with thin materials such as plywood and sheet metal. The 1 inch stroke is shorter than the DEWALT saws' 1-1/8 inch, so each cycle removes a little less, but the higher speed makes up for it in thin stock. A variable-speed trigger gives control for starting cuts.

The key point is platform cost. ONE+ batteries are widely available and inexpensive, so the saw is a bargain for homeowners who already own packs. Compared with the DEWALT DCS380B, the RYOBI is a lower-cost way into cordless, though it is less refined for daily use. If you need to cut a few branches or demolish a shed, it does the job.

Ownership: because it is a bare tool, you need ONE+ batteries. Keep blades sharp and match them to the material. Store the saw in a dry place, and check the clamp for wear. Pruning is where this saw shines, because a pruning blade with wide teeth zips through green limbs up to several inches thick without clogging.
products.bestFor: Homeowners with RYOBI ONE+ batteries who want a fast cordless saw for occasional demolition and pruning.
pros: 3,400 SPM is the fastest speed in the roundup
ONE+ batteries are widely available and inexpensive
Variable-speed trigger gives control for starting cuts
Works on wood, metal and branches
cons: Tool only, so batteries and a charger cost extra
Shorter 1 inch stroke clears chips less than 1-1/8 inch
Less refined for daily professional use

products.name: SKIL 9206-02 7.5 Amp Corded Reciprocating Saw
products.description:
A 7.5 amp motor is about 60 percent of the DEWALT DWE305's capacity, so this saw is aimed at light demolition, pruning and plumbing cuts. A heavy-duty metal gear housing adds ruggedness at a price where plastic gearboxes are common. Tool-less blade change keeps swaps quick.

The tradeoff is power. In thick or wet lumber and metal pipe, it slows sooner than the 12 amp DEWALT, and sustained demolition heats the motor. For occasional cuts such as trimming a pipe or pruning a limb, it is more than adequate. It is also the lowest-cost way to own a corded saw.

Ownership: use the right blade for the job, and let the saw reach speed before cutting. Check the cord, and blow out the vents after dusty work. A metal gear housing is a plus for durability, but grease levels still matter, so keep it dry and clean. Treat it as a light-duty saw and give it rest between long cuts, since a 7.5 amp motor runs warm in sustained cuts through dense material.
products.bestFor: Occasional users who need a corded saw for light cuts at the lowest cost.
pros: Metal gear housing adds ruggedness at a low price
Tool-less blade change is quick
Variable speed gives control for starting cuts
Lowest relative price among the corded options
cons: 7.5 amps slows in thick lumber and metal pipe

buyingCriteria.explanation: Stroke length is the distance the blade travels each cycle, and a longer stroke cuts faster and clears chips better. The DEWALT DCS380B and DCS387B have a 1-1/8 inch stroke, and the RYOBI has 1 inch. A short stroke binds in thick wood. A long stroke with a coarse blade is ideal for demolition. Always compare stroke and speed together, since a 1-1/8 inch stroke at 3,000 SPM moves the blade more than 3,000 feet in a minute of cutting, more than a short-stroke saw at the same SPM.

A corded saw draws amps, and the more it draws the more it can hold speed under load. The DEWALT DWE305 is 12 amps and the SKIL 9206-02 7.5. For nail-embedded lumber and pipe, aim for 10 amps or more. Many buyers choose a lighter saw and then find it stalls on the first stud. Check also that the cord is long enough for the job, because a thin extension cord drops voltage and causes the same bogging that a weak motor would.

A tool-free clamp changes blades in seconds, and a four-position clamp lets you rotate the blade for flush cuts. The DEWALT saws have both. A clamp that wears loose lets blades wobble. Check that it holds blades firmly. Rotating the blade 90 degrees is the trick that makes flush cuts possible, and it saves you from carrying a second tool.

A corded saw holds power without a battery fade, while a cordless saw gives freedom on ladders and roofs. The DEWALT DCS380B at 3,000 SPM approaches corded speed for short jobs. A compact cordless saw suits plumbing, and a corded saw suits all-day demolition. Remember that a cordless saw is only as good as its battery, so a 2.0 Ah pack will empty in a few minutes of metal cutting.

Reciprocating saws shake your arms, and a rubber grip and counterbalance reduce fatigue. The DCS380B has a rubber over-molded grip. A saw that vibrates heavily tires you in minutes. If you demolish for hours, vibration control is a bigger factor than speed, since sore hands slow you down more than a slower blade.

A pivoting shoe controls depth and spreads blade wear. The DCS380B has an adjustable pivoting shoe. A fixed shoe wears one section of the blade. A rafter hook is a nice extra for ladder work, though none of the picks here depend on it.

specDecoder.meaning: SPM is how many times the blade moves back and forth each minute. A higher number cuts faster in thin materials.
specDecoder.watchFor: The RYOBI's 3,400 SPM is a no-load number, and the shorter stroke offsets part of the speed. Do not compare SPM numbers across saws with different strokes.

specDecoder.meaning: This is the distance the blade travels, which sets how much material it removes per cycle.
specDecoder.watchFor: The DEWALT 1-1/8 inch stroke is longer than the RYOBI's 1 inch. Peak stroke length is only reached with the shoe pressed firmly against the work.

specDecoder.meaning: Amps measure current draw and indicate motor capacity for corded saws.
specDecoder.watchFor: The SKIL's 7.5 amps is not a match for the DEWALT's 12 amps in thick stock. A 12 amp saw draws more current on startup than a 7.5 amp saw, so check your extension cord rating.

specDecoder.meaning: Tool only means no battery or charger is included.
specDecoder.watchFor: The DEWALT DCS380B, DCS387B and RYOBI are tool only. Compare the bare tool price with a kit price before deciding.

specDecoder.meaning: Flush cutting means cutting against a surface, enabled by rotating the blade. A four-position clamp supports it.
specDecoder.watchFor: Only the DEWALT saws list a four-position clamp. Flush cutting still needs a blade short enough to clear the surface.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cutting speed and stroke
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared SPM and stroke length, from the SKIL's variable speed to the RYOBI's 3,400. Longer strokes earned credit for rough demolition. We treated every SPM figure as a no-load number and discounted it accordingly.

howWeEvaluated.title: Power source
howWeEvaluated.description: We split corded from cordless and weighed endurance against reach. The corded DEWALT DWE305 has the strongest motor. We weighed endurance as well as raw power, since a saw that cannot finish the job is not a bargain.

howWeEvaluated.title: Clamp and shoe
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at blade clamp and shoe design, which affect speed of use and blade life. Clamp wear is a common failure, so we favored designs that grip firmly after repeated changes.

howWeEvaluated.title: Size and weight
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the 14 inch DCS387B against full-size saws for tight spaces. The DCS387B's 14 inch length is the reference for tight spaces in this guide.

howWeEvaluated.title: Relative value
howWeEvaluated.description: We used price tier to compare what extra spending buys. We never compared listed prices, only relative tiers.

cards.label: Corded
cards.text: Steady power with no battery fade. The DEWALT DWE305 and SKIL 9206-02 fall here. They suit long jobs near outlets.

cards.label: Cordless
cards.text: Mobility on ladders and roofs, but packs drain on long jobs. The DEWALT DCS387B, DCS380B and RYOBI fall here.

howToChoose.note: Choose corded for all-day demolition and cordless for short jobs away from outlets.

howToChoose.subheading: For Cutting Pipe and Nail-Embedded Lumber Specifically

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Pipe and nails need a strong motor, a bi-metal blade and a firm shoe pressed against the work. Cut slowly to avoid blade breakage.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The DEWALT DWE305 handles pipe and nails best, and the DCS380B follows. The SKIL 9206-02 suits only light pipe.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You demolish for a living. The DEWALT DWE305 shows where durable corded saws start, and a brushless cordless saw is the next step.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You cut a few limbs a year. The SKIL 9206-02 or RYOBI covers that.

maintenance.why: A dull blade strains the motor. Fresh blades cut faster and cooler. Use a blade designed for the material to avoid heat and breakage.
Dust blocks the clamp from seating. A loose blade wobbles and breaks. Compressed air is the quickest way to clear it.
Damaged cords overheat. Replace at the first sign of wear. Wrap the cord loosely after use.
A worn shoe slips. Replace it if it wobbles. Look for cracks around the pivot.
Heat ages cells. Cool storage keeps capacity. Avoid leaving packs in a hot truck.

faq.q: Is cordless good enough for demolition?
faq.a: For short jobs, yes. A corded saw holds power for all-day work. Choose based on how long you cut. A fresh 5.0 Ah pack on a compact saw cuts through a surprising amount of 2x lumber.
It buys a heavy-duty corded saw or a cordless bare tool. Listing prices move, so check the live cost. Many buyers pair a corded saw with a compact cordless one.

faq.q: How long do these saws last?
faq.a: Heavy-duty corded saws last for years. Brushes and blades wear first.
Fewer teeth cut wood faster, and more teeth cut metal smoothly. Use a bi-metal blade for nails. Bi-metal blades survive nails and last longer than carbon steel ones.

faq.q: Why does my saw vibrate so much?
faq.a: Reciprocating motion causes vibration. A rubber grip and firm shoe contact reduce it. Holding the saw with both hands also reduces fatigue.

faq.q: Is it safe to cut pipe?
faq.a: Yes, if the pipe is drained and clamped. Wear eye protection. Turn off power at the breaker before cutting into walls.
